title: Credential Access
summary: Credential Access is the tactic covering the theft, guessing, or interception of account secrets, and it is frequently the single most valuable step in an intrusion because a valid credential can bypass controls that would stop everything else. Behaviours include brute force and password spraying against exposed authentication services, credential stuffing with data from unrelated breaches, dumping stored secrets from operating system memory or credential stores, reading browser and password manager databases, extracting keys and tokens from files, configuration stores, and container environments, intercepting authentication traffic, and abusing directory services to obtain or relay credentials. Defenders can see a great deal here if identity and endpoint telemetry is centralised. Repeated authentication failures followed by a success, logon attempts with unusual logon types, access to the memory of security-sensitive processes, bulk reads of credential files, suspicious use of directory replication or ticket-granting operations, and secrets exposed in code repositories all map to concrete events. The tactic remains hard to detect in isolation because spraying stays below account lockout thresholds by design, because legitimate administrators run the same tooling that attackers do, and because stolen credentials produce successful authentications that look healthy. Detection requires combining authentication analytics, endpoint behavioural monitoring, secret-scanning in source control, and monitoring of where secrets are stored, with priority given to protecting the highest-value credentials first.
objectives: Explain the main credential access paths, from spraying and stuffing to memory dumping and secret extraction, and how each generates evidence.
Analyse authentication telemetry to identify spraying and stuffing patterns that stay below lockout thresholds.
Identify endpoint behaviours that indicate credential dumping and explain what must be logged to see them.
Design secret-scanning and key-management controls that reduce the value of a stolen credential or key.
Prioritise protections for privileged, service, and machine identities rather than treating all accounts equally.
Build a triage path from a suspicious authentication to confirmation of credential theft and the actions taken with it.

beginner.definition: Credential access means stealing, guessing or intercepting the secrets that prove who someone is, such as passwords, keys and session tokens. A stolen credential is extremely useful, because the attacker then looks like a normal user. They may not need to break anything at all.
beginner.whyItMatters: Logging in with a real password bypasses most defenses, because the system thinks everything is fine. Attackers often prefer it to exploiting a bug. They also spread attempts across many accounts so no lockout rule triggers. If you ignore this step, a single leaked password can become a company-wide incident.
howItWorks: The attacker gathers possible usernames from public sources or from a previous data breach.
They try a few common passwords against many accounts, staying under the lockout limit.
On a machine they already control, they may read stored secrets from memory or saved files.
Each working password is tested to see how much access it really gives.
They reuse the best credentials to log in elsewhere, often without any tool at all.
beginner.example: Imagine an apartment block with one shared front door code. If a neighbor writes that code on a postcard, anyone who reads the postcard can walk in and out for weeks. The door still works perfectly, and the lock was never broken. Nobody looks suspicious, because everyone entering uses the correct code. Passwords work the same way. Once a valid password leaks, the front door opens politely for the wrong person.
takeaways: A stolen password often beats breaking in, because it looks legitimate.
Attackers guess slowly across many accounts to avoid triggering lockout rules.
Protect powerful accounts first and require a second proof of identity.
